name: Two-photon absorption
seoDesc: Two-photon absorption: work out laser power (P) from the wavelength and the focus size FWHM. A free chemistry calculator with the formula, units and a…
summary: Supply the wavelength, the focus size FWHM, the exposure time and the photon flux and the Two-photon absorption calculator solves for laser power (P). It is built for a bench calculation involving amounts, concentrations or reaction ratios. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Two-photon absorption calculator work?
sections.html:
The Two-photon absorption calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports laser power (P) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the wavelength (λ), the focus size FWHM, the exposure time (τ) and the photon flux (ϕ).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.html:

  • A measured quantity, entered by default in nanoseconds. The unit chip switches it to any of the 27 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in times 10 to the 24. The unit chip switches it to any of the 69 supported units.

sections.title: The formula behind the Two-photon absorption calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Laser power (P)=(6621486190496429 ÷ 9241962054000000000000000000000000000) × PI × (focus size FWHM ^ 2) × photon flux (ϕ) ÷ wavelength (λ)
Excitations per molecule (N)=(1 ÷ 200000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000) × cross-section (δ) × exposure time (τ) × (photon flux (ϕ) ^ 2)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in watts, and convertible to any of the 21 units on that chip.
  • A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Power, opening in watts
  • Length, opening in nanometers
  • Length, opening in micrometers
  • Time, opening in nanoseconds
  • Scientific notation, opening in times 10 to the 24

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Two-photon absorption calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Converting between the units a protocol and your bench equipment use
  • Preparing a solution and checking the numbers first
  • Working through a stoichiometry problem
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the wavelength, the focus size FWHM and the exposure time — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Two-photon absorption calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The unit chips cover the units listed on the page. A historical or regional unit that is missing can still be used by converting it to a listed unit first.
  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

faq.q: What does the Two-photon absorption calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns laser power (P), derived from the wavelength, the focus size FWHM and the exposure time. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Two-photon absorption calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the wavelength, the focus size FWHM, the exposure time and the photon flux, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter laser power (P) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Laser power (P) opens in watts and the chip beside it offers 21 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: Is the Two-photon absorption calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
